prompt: For sorting emails into folders, the team uses a small model that's cheaper and faster.
tells: a small model that's cheaper and faster
why: Simple jobs don't need the biggest model; a small one is quick and cheap. That's the size trade-off.
trap: Price is per token, but the decision is which size of model.

prompt: For tricky legal reasoning, they pay more for the largest model despite slower replies.
tells: pay more for the largest model despite slower replies
why: Bigger models are usually more capable but slower and costlier. Choosing one for hard tasks is the trade-off.
trap: A big model may also have a big window, but the clue is capability against cost and speed.

prompt: Easy questions go to a small model and hard ones to a large one.
tells: Easy questions go to a small model
why: Matching model size to difficulty saves money and time. That uses the size trade-off.
trap: It's routing by model size, not calling a tool.

prompt: A tiny model runs on the phone itself, giving instant replies but simpler answers.
tells: giving instant replies but simpler answers
why: Small models are fast and cheap enough to run on devices, but less capable. That's the trade-off.
trap: Speed and simplicity point to size, not memory.

prompt: The monthly bill tripled after switching every request to the biggest model.
tells: switching every request to the biggest model
why: Larger models cost more per request. Using the biggest everywhere shows the cost side of the trade-off.
trap: Tokens set the price, but the jump came from choosing a bigger model.

prompt: Users complained the chat felt slow, so the team tried a smaller model and kept quality acceptable.
why: Smaller models answer faster, trading a little capability for speed. That's the size trade-off.
